**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 95–97:**

﴿And do not exchange the covenant of God for a small price.﴾ That is, do not break your covenants, seeking through breaking them some small, fleeting gain of this world. Rather, fulfil them.

﴿Indeed, what is with God is﴾ the reward for you for fulfilling them, ﴿better for you, if you only knew.﴾ [The excess of one of the two exchanges over the other. Then he explained that,] saying: ﴿What is with you will end﴾, that is, the world and all that is in it will perish, ﴿but what is with God is lasting.﴾

﴿And We will surely reward﴾ [Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read وَلَنَجْزِيَنَّ with the nun (نَجْزِيَنَّ). The rest read it with the ya' (يَجْزِيَنَّ).] ﴿those who were patient﴾ in fulfilling their covenants, in ease and in hardship, ﴿their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾

Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Kharaqi informed us, who said: Abu al-Hasan al-Taysafuni informed us, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar al-Jawhari informed us, who said: Ahmad ibn 'Ali al-Kushmihani narrated to us, who said: 'Ali ibn Hujr narrated to us, who said: Isma'il ibn Ja'far narrated to us, who said: 'Amr ibn Abi 'Amr, the client of al-Muttalib, narrated to us, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves his worldly life harms his hereafter, and whoever loves his hereafter harms his worldly life. So prefer that which endures over that which perishes."[[Narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (4/308), who declared it sound according to the criteria of al-Bukhari and Muslim, but al-Dhahabi criticised him, saying that it has a break in its chain. It is also narrated by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad (4/175, 412), and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan (3/370). Sahib al-Mishkat attributed it to him in "Shu'ab al-Iman". Al-Haythami said: "Ahmad, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani narrated it, and its narrators are trustworthy." See Majma' al-Zawa'id (10/249), Mishkat al-Masabih no. (5179), and Kashf al-Khafa' wa Muzil al-Ilbas by al-'Ajluni (1/491). The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah (14/239).]]

His Exalted saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: it is lawful provision.

al-Hasan said: it is contentment.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: it means living in obedience (to God).

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it is the sweetness of obedience.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is Paradise. 'Awf narrated it from al-Hasan, and said: "Life is not good for anyone except in Paradise."[[After al-Tabari had cited the reports in explanation of this verse, he said: "The most correct of the sayings is the saying of the one who says: the interpretation of that is: 'We will surely cause him to live a good life' through contentment, because whoever God grants contentment with what He has apportioned to him of provision does not exhaust himself greatly for the world, does not toil extensively in it, and his life is not embittered in it by pursuing what remains of it that he missed, and by his greed for what he may never attain in it. As for the saying narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that it is lawful provision, it may mean what we have said, that He, the Exalted, makes him content in this world with what He provides him of lawful means, however little, so that his soul does not call him to much of it through unlawful means; not that He provides him with much lawful provision. For we have seen that most of those who act for God, the Exalted, by what pleases Him, have not been given much lawful provision in this world, and we have found that narrowness of living is more prevalent among them than abundance." See Tafsir al-Tabari (14/172).]]

﴿And We will surely reward them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾

Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Kharaqi informed us, who said: Abu al-Hasan al-Taysafuni informed us, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar al-Jawhari informed us, who said: Ahmad ibn 'Ali al-Kushmihani narrated to us, who said: 'Ali ibn Hujr narrated to us, who said: Isma'il ibn Ja'far narrated to us, who said: 'Amr ibn Abi 'Amr, the client of al-Muttalib, narrated to us, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves his worldly life harms his hereafter, and whoever loves his hereafter harms his worldly life. So prefer that which endures over that which perishes."[[Narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (4/308), who declared it sound according to the criteria of al-Bukhari and Muslim, but al-Dhahabi criticised him, saying that it has a break in its chain. It is also narrated by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad (4/175, 412), and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan (3/370). Sahib al-Mishkat attributed it to him in "Shu'ab al-Iman". Al-Haythami said: "Ahmad, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani narrated it, and its narrators are trustworthy." See Majma' al-Zawa'id (10/249), Mishkat al-Masabih no. (5179), and Kashf al-Khafa' wa Muzil al-Ilbas by al-'Ajluni (1/491). The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah (14/239).]]

His Exalted saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life.﴾ Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: it is lawful provision.

al-Hasan said: it is contentment.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: it means living in obedience (to God).

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: it is the sweetness of obedience.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is Paradise. 'Awf narrated it from al-Hasan, and said: "Life is not good for anyone except in Paradise."[[After al-Tabari had cited the reports in explanation of this verse, he said: "The most correct of the sayings is the saying of the one who says: the interpretation of that is: 'We will surely cause him to live a good life' through contentment, because whoever God grants contentment with what He has apportioned to him of provision does not exhaust himself greatly for the world, does not toil extensively in it, and his life is not embittered in it by pursuing what remains of it that he missed, and by his greed for what he may never attain in it. As for the saying narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that it is lawful provision, it may mean what we have said, that He, the Exalted, makes him content in this world with what He provides him of lawful means, however little, so that his soul does not call him to much of it through unlawful means; not that He provides him with much lawful provision. For we have seen that most of those who act for God, the Exalted, by what pleases Him, have not been given much lawful provision in this world, and we have found that narrowness of living is more prevalent among them than abundance." See Tafsir al-Tabari (14/172).]]

﴿And We will surely reward them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 98:

His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾, meaning: when you intend to recite the Qur'an, ﴿seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed﴾, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you rise to prayer, then wash﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

Seeking refuge (al-isti'adhah) is a sunnah when reciting the Qur'an [[Al-Tabari said (14/173): "His saying, 'So seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed,' is not a binding command; rather it is an informing and a recommendation, because there is no disagreement among all that whoever recites the Qur'an without seeking refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed, before or after his recitation, has not neglected an obligatory duty." Ibn al-Jawzi said in Zad al-Masir (4/490): "Seeking refuge during recitation is a sunnah, in prayer and outside it." Ibn 'Atiyyah said (8/507): "Al-Naqqash related from 'Ata' that seeking refuge is obligatory." See also: Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/15, 2/587; al-Majmu' of al-Nawawi: 3/284; and al-Tibyan fi Adab Hamalat al-Qur'an of al-Nawawi, pp. 64–65.]].

Most scholars hold that seeking refuge is before the recitation [[See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 14/173; al-Qurtubi: 10/174–175; al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8/507; Ahkam al-Qur'an of Ibn al-Arabi: 3/1175.]].

Abu Hurayrah said: it is after it [[Al-Nawawi in al-Majmu' (3/284) transmitted this from Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Sirin and al-Nakha'i, and that Abu Hurayrah used to seek refuge after finishing al-Fatihah, based on the apparent wording of the verse. The correct view is the first opinion, before the recitation, due to the hadiths indicating that it precedes the recitation. See also: Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/13–15, 2/587; Ahkam al-Qur'an of Ibn al-Arabi: 3/1175.]].

Its wording is that he says: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan."

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Malihi informed us, Abu Muhammad Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi informed us, Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated to us, Shu'bah informed us, from Amr ibn Murrah, I heard Asim, from Ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, that he saw the Prophet ﷺ praying. He said: he said "Allahu akbar" [three times], "Allahu akbar kabiran" [three times], [and "Al-hamdu lillahi kathiran" three times, and "Subhan Allahi bukratan wa asilan" three times], "Allahumma inni a'udhu bika min al-shaytan al-rajim, min hamzihi wa nafkhihi wa nafthihi."

Amr said: His nafkh is pride, his nafth is poetry, and his hamz is madness (al-mawtah), and al-mawtah is insanity. Seeking refuge in Allah is holding fast to Him [[Related by Abu Dawud in the Prayer, chapter on what is said to open the prayer of supplication: 1/372; Ibn Majah in the Establishment of Prayer, chapter on no seeking refuge in prayer: 1/265; authenticated by Ibn Hibban, p. 123 of Mawarid al-Zam'an; al-Hakim: 1/235; also related by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad: 4/80, and by the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 3/43.]].

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 99–101:**

﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾, meaning proof and dominion, ﴿over those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾. Sufyan said: He has no authority to lead them into a sin that will not be forgiven.

﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾, meaning they obey him and enter into his guardianship, ﴿and those who associate others with Him﴾. That is, they associate others with Allah. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Satan, and the implied meaning is those who, because of him, associate others with Allah.

﴿And when We substitute one verse for another﴾, meaning when We abrogate the ruling of one verse and replace it with another ruling, ﴿and Allah knows best what He sends down﴾, meaning He knows best what is most beneficial for His creation in what He changes and substitutes of His rulings, ﴿they say, "You are only a fabricator"﴾, O Muhammad, meaning an inventor of lies. This is because the polytheists said: Muhammad mocks his companions. He commands them today to do one thing and forbids it to them tomorrow. He is only a fabricator who invents it from his own self [[See: Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, p. 325.]].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ the reality of the Qur'an and the explanation of the abrogating (nasikh) from the abrogated (mansukh).

He means the Qur'an, and "the Holy Spirit" is Jibril; "in truth" means "with sincerity." **"To strengthen those who believe"** (﴿لِيُثَبِّتَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾), that is, to strengthen the hearts of the believers so that they increase in faith and certainty, **"and as guidance and good news for the Muslims"** (﴿وَهُدًى وَبُشْرَى لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ﴾).

**"We know well that they say: 'Only a human being teaches him'"** (﴿وَلَقَدْ نَعْلَمُ أَنَّهُمْ يَقُولُونَ إِنَّمَا يُعَلِّمُهُ بَشَرٌ﴾), a mortal man, and that it is not from Allah. The commentators differed about who this human was.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach a smith (*qayn*) in Makkah named "Balʿam." He was a Christian, and his tongue was non-Arabic (*a'jamī*). The polytheists saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entering and leaving his place, so they said: "Only Balʿam teaches him." [Narrated by Ibn Jarir, 14/177. al-Suyuti attributed it also to Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh with a weak chain. Al-Durr al-Manthur 5/167; Zad al-Masir 4/492.]

'Ikrimah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to teach a boy belonging to the Banu al-Mughirah called "Ya'ish" [In al-Durr al-Manthur it reads "Muqays," and it is probably a copyist's error]. He used to read the scriptures, so the Quraysh said: "Only Ya'ish teaches him." [Narrated by Ibn Jarir from 'Ikrimah, 14/178; see Zad al-Masir 4/492.]

Al-Farra' said: The polytheists said: "He only learns from 'Ayesh, a slave who belonged to Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza. He had become Muslim and his Islam was good, and his tongue was non-Arabic." [The same was also said by al-Zajjaj; see Zad al-Masir 4/492.]

Ibn Ishaq said: As it reached me, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) often sat near Marwah with a Christian Roman boy, a slave of one of the Banu al-Hadrami, called "Jabr," who used to read the scriptures. [Narrated by al-Tabari, 14/178.]

'Abd Allah ibn Muslim al-Hadrami said: We had two slaves from the people of 'Ayn al-Tamr, one called Yasar, who was given the kunya "Abu Fukayhah," and the other called "Jabr." They used to make swords in Makkah, and they used to read the Torah and the Gospel. The Prophet (ﷺ) would sometimes pass by them while they were reading, so he would stop and listen.

al-Dahhak said: Whenever the disbelievers harmed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would sit with them and find comfort in their speech. So the polytheists said: "Muhammad only learns from them," and this verse was revealed. [Narrated by al-Tabari, 14/178; al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul p. 326; see Zad al-Masir 4/493.]

Allah the Exalted said, refuting them: **"The tongue of the one they point to is foreign"** (﴿لِسَانُ الَّذِي يُلْحِدُونَ إِلَيْهِ ... أَعْجَمِيٌّ﴾). That is, they incline toward and point to him. "Foreign" (*a'jamī*) refers to one who is not eloquent, even if he dwells among the Arabs of the desert. The word *ajamī* is attributed to the non-Arabs (*ajam*), even if he is eloquent. The *a'rabī* is the Bedouin, and the *'arabī* is attributed to the Arabs, even if he is not eloquent. **"And this is a clear Arabic tongue"** (﴿وَهَذَا لِسَانٌ عَرَبِيٌّ مُبِينٌ﴾), that is, eloquent. By "tongue" he means the Qur'an, and the Arabs say "lughah" (language) is "lisan" (tongue).

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 16, verses 104–106:**

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them﴾ meaning, Allah will not give them guidance. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment.﴾ Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that the disbelievers are the fabricators (al-muftarun). He said: ﴿Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies, and it is they who are the liars﴾, not Muhammad (ﷺ).

If it is said: He said, "Only those who do not believe fabricate lies," so what is the meaning of His saying, "And it is they who are the liars"? It is said: "Only they fabricate lies" is a report about their action, and "and it is they who are the liars" is a description that is inherent in them, like a man's saying to another: "You have lied, and you are a liar," meaning: you lied in this statement, and lying is your habit.

Abu Sa'id al-Shurayhi informed us, Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us, Abu Hafs Umar ibn Ahmad al-Jawhari informed us, my grandfather Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Umar ibn Hafs informed us, Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Faraj al-Azraq narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far narrated to us, Ya'la ibn al-Ashdaq narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Jarad, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, does the believer commit adultery?" He said, "It may happen." He said: I said, "Does the believer steal?" He said, "It may happen." I said, "Does the believer lie?" He said, "No." Allah says: "Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies."[[Narrated by al-Kharai'ti in Masawi' al-Akhlaq, p. 69, edited by Abu al-Nasr Shalabi. Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/168) attributed it to Ibn Asakir in his History. In its chain is Ya'la ibn al-Ashdaq al-Uqayli; Abu Hatim said: "He is worthless, weak in narration." Ibn Hibban said: "Narration from him is not permissible under any circumstances, nor is it valid as proof." See al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil (9/303), al-Majruhin by Ibn Hibban (3/142).]]

﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who has been compelled while his heart remains firm in faith﴾

Ibn Abbas said: This verse was revealed concerning Ammar, because the polytheists seized him, and his father Yasir, his mother Sumayya, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab, and Salim, and they tortured them. As for Sumayya, she was tied between two camels and struck in her private part with a spear, and she was killed, and her husband Yasir was killed; they were the first two people killed in Islam. As for Ammar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue, under compulsion.[[See: Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, p. 326; Tafsir al-Tabari (14/181); al-Mustadrak (2/357); al-Durr al-Manthur (5/169–170).]]

Qatadah said: The sons of al-Mughirah seized Ammar, dipped him in the well of Maymun, and said to him, "Disbelieve in Muhammad." So he complied with them in that, while his heart was averse to it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed that Ammar had disbelieved, and he said, "No indeed! Ammar is filled with faith from his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then Ammar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "What is behind you?" He said, "Evil, O Messenger of Allah. I spoke against you and mentioned their gods." He said, "How did you find your heart?" He said, "Reassured in faith." So the Prophet (ﷺ) began wiping his eyes and said, "If they return to you, then return to them with what you said." Then this verse was revealed.[[Narrated by al-Tabari (14/181), Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and al-Hakim. See: al-Durr al-Manthur (5/172), al-Qurtubi (10/181), al-Mustadrak (2/357).]]

Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning some people from Makkah who believed. Some companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to them: "Emigrate, for we will not consider you among us until you emigrate to us." So they set out intending Madinah, but Quraysh overtook them on the road, and they disbelieved under compulsion.[[Narrated by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim. See: al-Durr al-Manthur (5/171).]]

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Jabr, the freedman of Amir ibn al-Hadrami, whose master compelled him to disbelieve, so he disbelieved under compulsion.[[See: Zad al-Masir (4/495–496).]]

﴿while his heart is reassured in faith.﴾ Then the freedman of Jabr embraced Islam, his Islam became good, and Jabr emigrated with his master.

﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾ meaning: opens his chest to disbelief by accepting it and choosing it, ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾

The scholars agreed that whoever is compelled to utter a word of disbelief may say it with his tongue, and if he says it with his tongue without believing in it, it is not disbelief. And if he refuses to say it until he is killed, that is better.[[See: Tafsir al-Tabari (14/182); al-Qurtubi (10/181, 188–190); Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas (4/13–14); Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-'Arabi (3/1177–1179); Zad al-Masir (4/496); Tafsir Ibn Kathir (2/589).]]

The scholars differed concerning the divorce of one who is compelled. Most of them held that it does not take effect.[[Al-Shafi'i, Malik, and Ahmad said: The divorce of one who is compelled does not take effect; this is also narrated from Umar, Ali, and Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned it from Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ata', Tawus, al-Hasan, Shurayh, al-Qasim, Salim, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Abu Hanifah permitted it, saying: The divorce of one who is compelled takes effect, because he has not been deprived of more than consent, and its existence is not a condition for divorce. This is also narrated from al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Abu Qilabah, al-Zuhri, and Qatadah. For details see: Tafsir al-Qurtubi (10/184); Zad al-Masir (4/497); Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas (5/14–15); Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-'Arabi (3/1181).]]

He said, "It may happen." He said: I said, "Does the believer steal?" He said, "It may happen." I said, "Does the believer lie?" He said, "No." Allah says: "Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies."[[Narrated by al-Kharai'ti in Masawi' al-Akhlaq, p. 69, edited by Abu al-Nasr Shalabi. Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/168) attributed it to Ibn Asakir in his History. In its chain is Ya'la ibn al-Ashdaq al-Uqayli; Abu Hatim said: "He is worthless, weak in narration." ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who has been compelled while his heart remains firm in faith﴾

Ibn Abbas said: This verse was revealed concerning Ammar, because the polytheists seized him, and his father Yasir, his mother Sumayya, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab, and Salim, and they tortured them. As for Sumayya, she was tied between two camels and struck in her private part with a spear, and she was killed, and her husband Yasir was killed; they were the first two people killed in Islam. As for Ammar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue, under compulsion.[[See: Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, p. 326; Tafsir al-Tabari (14/181); al-Mustadrak (2/357); al-Durr al-Manthur (5/169–170).]]

Qatadah said: The sons of al-Mughirah seized Ammar, dipped him in the well of Maymun, and said to him, "Disbelieve in Muhammad." So he complied with them in that, while his heart was averse to it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed that Ammar had disbelieved, and he said, "No indeed! Ammar is filled with faith from his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then Ammar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "What is behind you?" He said, "Evil, O Messenger of Allah. I spoke against you and mentioned their gods." Some companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to them: "Emigrate, for we will not consider you among us until you emigrate to us." Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Jabr, the freedman of Amir ibn al-Hadrami, whose master compelled him to disbelieve, so he disbelieved under compulsion.[[See: Zad al-Masir (4/495–496).]]

﴿while his heart is reassured in faith.﴾ Then the freedman of Jabr embraced Islam, his Islam became good, and Jabr emigrated with his master.

﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾ meaning: opens his chest to disbelief by accepting it and choosing it, ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾

The scholars agreed that whoever is compelled to utter a word of disbelief may say it with his tongue, and if he says it with his tongue without believing in it, it is not disbelief. And if he refuses to say it until he is killed, that is better.[[See: Tafsir al-Tabari (14/182); al-Qurtubi (10/181, 188–190); Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas (4/13–14); Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-'Arabi (3/1177–1179); Zad al-Masir (4/496); Tafsir Ibn Kathir (2/589).]]

The scholars differed concerning the divorce of one who is compelled. Most of them held that it does not take effect.[[Al-Shafi'i, Malik, and Ahmad said: The divorce of one who is compelled does not take effect; this is also narrated from Umar, Ali, and Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned it from Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ata', Tawus, al-Hasan, Shurayh, al-Qasim, Salim, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Abu Hanifah permitted it, saying: The divorce of one who is compelled takes effect, because he has not been deprived of more than consent, and its existence is not a condition for divorce. This is also narrated from al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Abu Qilabah, al-Zuhri, and Qatadah. For details see: Tafsir al-Qurtubi (10/184); Zad al-Masir (4/497); Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas (5/14–15); Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-'Arabi (3/1181).]]

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 16, verses 111–112:**

﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾: arguing and making its case, ﴿for itself﴾, for what it sent forward of good and evil, preoccupied with itself and having no leisure for anything else. ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged.﴾

It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to Kaʿb al-Ahbar: "Frighten us." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, by Him in whose hand my soul is, if you came on the Day of Resurrection with the deeds of seventy prophets, there would still come over you moments in which nothing concerns you but your own soul. Indeed, Hell has a roar, and no angel brought near and no prophet sent and chosen will remain but that he will fall to his knees, even Ibrahim, the Friend of the Merciful, who will say: 'O Lord, I ask You for nothing but my own soul.'" The proof of this is what Allah revealed to you: ﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾ [[al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/173) as narrated by Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in "al-Zuhd," ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Kaʿb al-Ahbar. See also Zad al-Masir: 4/499, and Ruh al-Maʿani: 14/240–241.]].

ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding this verse that he said: "The dispute among people on the Day of Resurrection will not cease until the soul disputes with the body. The soul will say: 'O Lord, I had no hand with which to strike, nor a foot with which to walk, nor an eye with which to see.' The body will say: 'You created me like wood, with no hand for me to strike with, nor a foot to walk with, nor an eye to see with. Then this (light) came, like a ray of light, and by it my tongue spoke, my eye saw, and my foot walked.' So Allah will strike for them both a parable: a blind man and a lame man who entered a garden containing fruit. The blind man cannot see the fruit, and the lame man cannot reach it. So the blind man carried the lame man, and they both ate some of the fruit, and upon them both is the punishment."

[[al-Alusi said (14/241): "The apparent meaning is that this report from the scholar Ibn ʿAbbas is not sound, and he is too exalted to have the 'arguing' in the verse interpreted as what was mentioned. The truth is that it indicates nothing except lack of concern." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said (8/525): "The apparent meaning of the verse is that every soul argues, whether believing or disbelieving. When the disbelievers argue with their lies and their denial of disbelief, the limbs and the messengers and others testify against them according to their groups, and then they will not speak ﴿nor will they be permitted to make excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. Thus the verses of the Qur'an are reconciled according to the different situations." Another group said: "The saying of every individual, prophets and others, is: 'Myself, myself.' This is not arguing or making a case, but merely a wish."]]

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town that was secure and at rest﴾, meaning Mecca, which was secure, its people not raided and no attacks made upon it, ﴿at rest﴾, settled with its people, not needing to move about in search of pasture as the rest of the Arabs needed to. ﴿Its provision came to it in abundance from every place﴾: it was brought to it by land and sea. A parallel is His words: ﴿to which are brought the fruits of all things﴾ [al-Qasas: 57].

﴿But it denied the blessings of Allah﴾: ﴿ni'am﴾ is the plural of ﴿ni'mah﴾ (blessing). It was also said that it is the plural of ﴿na'ma'﴾, like ﴿ba'sa'﴾ (hardship) and ﴿ab'us﴾ (distresses). ﴿So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger﴾: Allah tested them with hunger for seven years, and the Arabs cut off their supplies (al-mirah, the provisions and trade) by the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), until they suffered greatly, and ate burnt bones, carrion, dead dogs, and ʿihn, which is wool treated with blood. **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 16, verses 111–112:**

﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾: arguing and making its case, ﴿for itself﴾, for what it sent forward of good and evil, preoccupied with itself and having no leisure for anything else. ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged.﴾

It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to Kaʿb al-Ahbar: "Frighten us." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, by Him in whose hand my soul is, if you came on the Day of Resurrection with the deeds of seventy prophets, there would still come over you moments in which nothing concerns you but your own soul. Indeed, Hell has a roar, and no angel brought near and no prophet sent and chosen will remain but that he will fall to his knees, even Ibrahim, the Friend of the Merciful, who will say: 'O Lord, I ask You for nothing but my own soul.'" The proof of this is what Allah revealed to you: ﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾ [[al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/173) as narrated by Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in "al-Zuhd," ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Kaʿb al-Ahbar. See also Zad al-Masir: 4/499, and Ruh al-Maʿani: 14/240–241.]].

ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding this verse that he said: "The dispute among people on the Day of Resurrection will not cease until the soul disputes with the body. The soul will say: 'O Lord, I had no hand with which to strike, nor a foot with which to walk, nor an eye with which to see.' The body will say: 'You created me like wood, with no hand for me to strike with, nor a foot to walk with, nor an eye to see with. Then this (light) came, like a ray of light, and by it my tongue spoke, my eye saw, and my foot walked.' So Allah will strike for them both a parable: a blind man and a lame man who entered a garden containing fruit. The blind man cannot see the fruit, and the lame man cannot reach it. So the blind man carried the lame man, and they both ate some of the fruit, and upon them both is the punishment."

[[al-Alusi said (14/241): "The apparent meaning is that this report from the scholar Ibn ʿAbbas is not sound, and he is too exalted to have the 'arguing' in the verse interpreted as what was mentioned. The truth is that it indicates nothing except lack of concern." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said (8/525): "The apparent meaning of the verse is that every soul argues, whether believing or disbelieving. This is not arguing or making a case, but merely a wish."]]

The scholars of legal theory (ahl al-usul) said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to follow the sacred law (shari'ah) of Abraham, except what was abrogated in his own law, and what was not abrogated became law for him.[[For detail see: Ibn Hazm's al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam: 5/722 onward; al-Qurtubi's Tafsir: 10/198.]] God's statement: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed about it.﴾ It was said: its meaning is that the Sabbath was only made a curse upon those who differed about it, that is, who opposed it.

It was also said: its meaning is that God did not impose the glorification and prohibition of the Sabbath except upon those who differed about it, that is, who opposed it. Some people said: it is the greatest day, because God finished creating things on Friday and then rested on Saturday. Others said: rather, the greatest day is Sunday, because God began the creation of things on it. They chose to glorify a day other than the one God had prescribed for them, whereas God had prescribed for them the glorification of Friday.

Al-Kalbi said: Moses, peace be upon him, commanded them regarding Friday. He said: "Devote yourselves to God one day in every seven days, worship Him on Friday, do not work on it for your trades, and work six days for your trades." But they refused and said: "We want only the day on which God finished the creation, which is Saturday." So God made that day obligatory for them and made it strict upon them. Then Jesus, peace be upon him, brought them Friday, but they said: "We do not want their festival to come after our festival" (meaning the Jews), so they adopted Sunday. Then God gave Friday to this community, and they accepted it, and blessing was granted to them in it.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 125:**

﴿Summon to the way of your Lord with wisdom﴾ — with the Qur'an. ﴿And fair admonition﴾ — meaning the admonitions of the Qur'an.

It has also been said: the fair admonition is calling to God through encouragement (*targhib*) and warning (*tarhib*).

It has also been said: it is gentle, tender speech, without harshness or rebuke.

﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ — and dispute and debate with them in the best manner of disputation. That is, turn away from their harm, and do not fall short in conveying the message and calling to the truth. It was abrogated (*nasakhat*, i.e. made *mansukh*, abrogated) by the verse of fighting [[This noble verse was revealed in Mecca at a time when the command was to reconcile with the polytheists. God Most High commanded His Prophet ﷺ to call to the religion of God and His law gently and mildly, without harshness and rebuke, and in this manner Muslims should be admonished until the Day of Resurrection. It is therefore *muhkam* (clear and definitive, i.e. not abrogated) concerning the disobedient among the monotheists, and *mansukh* (abrogated) concerning the disbelievers by the command to fight. It has been said: whoever among the disbelievers can be reached by these means, and whose faith is hoped for without fighting, then the verse is *muhkam* in his case, and God knows best. Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10 / 200; the original wording is from Ibn 'Atiyyah in al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8 / 546. See also the commentary on verse (3) of surah al-Hijr: 4 / 368, note (6), and 3 / 373, note (2).]].

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 126:

﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾. These verses were revealed in Medina concerning the martyrs of Uhud [[Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: (4 / 546): The people of tafsir are unanimous that this verse is Medinan, revealed concerning the mutilation of Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him, on the day of Uhud. This is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and in the books of biography (siyar). al-Nahhas, however, held that it is Meccan. See also: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10 / 201.]] . That is because when the Muslims saw what the polytheists had done to their slain on the day of Uhud, namely ripping open the bellies and the vile mutilation, until no one among the Muslim dead remained unmutilated except Hanzala ibn al-Rahib, for his father Abu ʿAmir al-Rahib was with Abu Sufyan, so they left Hanzala on that account, the Muslims said when they saw that: "If Allah grants us victory over them, we will surpass what they did, and we will mutilate them with a mutilation such as no one among the Arabs has inflicted on anyone." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood over his paternal uncle Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, whose nose and ears had been cut off, whose genitals had been severed, and whose belly had been split open. Hind bint ʿUtba took a piece of his liver and chewed it, then she tried to swallow it, but it did not remain in her stomach until she spat it out. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Indeed, if she had eaten it, she would never have entered the Fire; Hamza is too honoured by Allah the Exalted for any part of his body to enter the Fire." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at his uncle Hamza and saw something that had never pained his heart more than that sight, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May the mercy of Allah be upon you, for to the best of my knowledge you were always doing good deeds and keeping the ties of kinship. Were it not for the grief that would follow you, it would have pleased me to leave you until you are gathered from scattered tribes. By Allah, if Allah grants me victory over them, I will mutilate seventy of them in your place." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And if you punish, then punish﴾, the verse.

﴿And if you are patient, it is better for those who are patient﴾. That is: and if you pardon, it is better for those who pardon. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: "Rather, we will be patient," and he refrained from what he had intended and made expiation for his oath.[[This narration was cited by al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, pp. 329–330, from the exegetes without giving a chain of transmission, and al-Khazin did likewise in his tafsir: 4 / 131. Within this context there is what is sound and what is weak. Here are some of the narrations on this: From Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: When it was the day of Uhud, forty-four men of the Ansar were struck, and six of the Muhajirun, among them Hamza, and they were mutilated. The Ansar said: "If we gain a victory over them on a day like this, we will surpass them." He said: When it was the day of the conquest of Mecca, Allah the Exalted revealed: "And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished, and if you are patient, it is better for those who are patient." A man said: "There will be no Quraysh after today." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hold back from the people except for four." Related by al-Tirmidhi in the Tafsir: 8 / 559–560, who said: This is a hasan gharib hadith; Ibn Hibban related it, as in Mawarid al-Zaman p. 411; al-Hakim authenticated it in al-Mustadrak: 2 / 359 and 446, and al-Dhahabi agreed with him; al-Tabarani in al-Kabir: 3 / 157; ʿAbd Allah ibn Imam Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad: 5 / 135; al-Suyuti attributed it to al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar pointed to this narration and said in al-Fath (7 / 372): "These chains strengthen one another." al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani related, with a chain containing weakness, from Abu Hurayra that when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw Hamza mutilated he said: "May the mercy of Allah be upon you..." — as in the author's context. See: Fath al-Bari: 7 / 371; and consult: Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd: 3 / 12–13; Sirat Ibn Hisham: 2 / 91, 95–96; Imta' al-Asma' of al-Maqrizi p. 153; Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi pp. 329–331, which contains all the narrations; likewise al-Durr al-Manthur: 5 / 178–179; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2 / 592.]].

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak said: This was before the revelation of Bara'a, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to fight those who fought him and was forbidden to initiate fighting. When Allah made Islam and its people mighty, Bara'a was revealed, and they were commanded to wage jihad, and this verse was abrogated [[Related by al-Tabari from Ibn ʿAbbas: 14 / 196; see also: al-Durr al-Manthur: 5 / 180; Zad al-Masir: 4 / 508.]].

Al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri, Mujahid and Ibn Sirin said: The verse is muhkam (non-abrogated), revealed concerning one who has been wronged with an injustice; it is not lawful for him to take from his wrongdoer more than what the wrongdoer took from him. He is commanded to requite or to pardon, and forbidden from transgression [[al-Tabari: 14 / 197; al-Qurtubi: 10 / 201; al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8 / 548; Zad al-Masir: 4 / 508. Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The correct view on this is that Allah the Exalted commanded those among the believers who were punished with a punishment that they may punish the one who punished them with the like of what he was punished with, if they choose that punishment, and He informed him that patience in abstaining from punishing him is better for him than what he did, and He resolved upon His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient. That is because this is the apparent meaning of the revelation, and the interpretations which we have mentioned from those who related them are all possible readings of the verse. Since this is so, and there is no indication in the verse, from report or reason, as to which of these was meant, it is obligatory upon us to rule by it, and to say: it is a muhkam verse, by which Allah the Exalted commanded His servants not to transgress, in what is due to them before others, of rights of property or life, beyond the right which Allah has assigned to them, and that it is not abrogated, since there is no indication of its abrogation, and that the statement that it is muhkam has a sound and understandable basis.]].

Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ):

﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except through Allah﴾, i.e., by Allah's help and His enabling. ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ at their turning away from you. ﴿And do not be in distress over what they plot﴾, i.e., over the deeds they committed.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿ضِيقٍ﴾ here and in An-Naml with a kasra on the dad (*ḍīqin*). The others read it with a fatha on the dad (*ḍayqin*). The scholars of Kufa said: both are dialectal variants, like *ritl* and *ratl* (a unit of weight).

Abu 'Amr said: *al-ḍayq* with a fatha means grief, and with a kasra means hardship.

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-ḍīq* with a kasra refers to scarcity of livelihood and to dwellings, whereas what is in the heart and breast is with a fatha.

Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ḍayq* is a lightened form of *ḍayyiq*, like *hayn* and *hayyin*, and *layn* and *layyin*. On this view it is an adjective, as if he had said: "and do not be in a difficult matter arising from their plotting."

﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who are mindful of Him﴾, by avoiding what is forbidden, ﴿and those who are doers of good﴾ through aid and support.
